title: The Arrows Between Three Colors
teaser: In two weeks, Lin Lan will lead a Saturday supermarket shift on her own for the first time. Her course hours, shadowing, and on-the-job practice are all close to their planned totals, yet when the lunchtime rush actually arrives, the three colors on her phone still cannot tell her where to place each employee.
paragraphs: At 12:30 on Saturday, the checkout line stretches past the promotion display, while two out-of-stock alerts come through her headset almost at the same time. Lin Lan has two weeks left before she must lead a full shift on her own, and today is one of her practice shifts. She glances at her phone calendar. On-the-job practice, learning from a senior colleague, and formal courses each have their own color, and beside the month-end total she has written the 70, 20, and 10 percentages she calculated for herself. The three blocks are almost all complete as planned. None of them, however, can make the decision she now has only minutes to make: pull someone away to open a fifth checkout, or keep that person available for shelves and self-checkout.

She moves one shelf-stocking employee to the tills. The line shortens quickly and customers begin moving forward; in the most visible part of the store, the decision works at once. Ten or fifteen minutes later, however, both the drinks section and the ready-to-eat shelves develop gaps, and another employee has to move back and forth covering them. There are no serious complaints that day, and Lin Lan does not regard the shift as a failure. After work, she ticks off all three learning activities as planned. Then she notices that her “learning from a senior colleague” time is still forty minutes short, so she books another forty-minute conversation. The calendar looks more complete, while the judgment she made at 12:30 remains at the store and never enters the other two colored boxes.

On Monday, Sister Zhou does not spend forty minutes delivering experience from the beginning. Instead, she asks Lin Lan to bring out the staffing record from Saturday and the training card from the course. Lin Lan can say how long the queue was, but she cannot remember the ratio of shopping carts to baskets, and she did not include the first out-of-stock alert in her judgment. The training card specifically asks learners to distinguish “temporary checkout congestion” from “a rise in traffic across the whole store.” Lin Lan had answered that exercise correctly during the course. On her phone, she renames “forty-minute conversation” as “review the 12:30 decision.” For the first time, one course tool, one real decision, and Sister Zhou’s feedback are placed around the same problem.

On Tuesday, she goes back through the decision card and writes the two out-of-stock alerts from Saturday in the margin. On Thursday, she takes only this one judgment to Sister Zhou and asks which signal is easiest to miss. The second Saturday, traffic begins rising again. Lin Lan does not repeat the previous week’s move. She opens only one temporary checkout and keeps one mobile employee free for shelves and the self-checkout area. The queue shortens without the shelves developing the same gaps as before. Half an hour later, however, one self-checkout machine fails. Lin Lan forgets to subtract that machine from the available capacity, and the main line briefly grows again.

This time, she does not add another vague block of “discussion hours.” After the shift, she writes, “A self-checkout failure pushes people back into the main queue,” on the operating record. On Monday, when she looks through the course material, she marks the same point beside “capacity change.” In her next session, Sister Zhou spends only fifteen minutes with her on one question: if that signal had appeared earlier, which position should have moved first? The three learning sources still remain distinct. None is removed, and no extra total time is added. But the same real problem now leaves traces in all three places.

Two weeks later, during Lin Lan’s first independent Saturday, the line grows again at 12:30. Before moving anyone, she checks the basket-to-cart ratio, the out-of-stock alerts, and the number of functioning self-checkout machines. When the busiest period has passed, she returns to the staff room and opens her phone calendar. All three colors are still there, and she has not erased the 70, 20, 10 line at the end of the month. Only “make up 40 minutes” has been crossed out. Between the course, the review, and the next shift, she draws a small arrow in each gap. The last arrow points back to 12:30 next Saturday.
concept: The 70-20-10 learning framework uses three broad sources to help explain development: challenging work experience, developmental relationships with other people, and formal learning such as courses. The 70, 20, and 10 figures are better treated as heuristic proportions than as a personal time formula that must be calculated precisely. What matters is not only whether all three sources exist, but whether they connect around the same capability problem, so that experience produces questions, feedback helps interpret them, formal learning provides structure, and the cycle returns to new practice.
explanation: Lin Lan’s problem is not a shortage of learning time, nor are formal courses or feedback ineffective. At the beginning, all three types of activity are already happening as planned, and she can even add time until the target proportions are met. But each activity ends inside its own calendar block: the problem exposed on the shop floor does not enter the course material, and the course tool does not enter the next real decision. The visible result of the first shift is that the queue shrinks quickly and her learning hours continue to reach their targets. The real result is that she still acts on only one conspicuous signal. The behavioral turn occurs when the same 12:30 event starts moving through all three learning sources. The second shift still contains a new mistake involving the self-checkout machine, which shows that the framework does not guarantee one-step mastery. What matters is that the new problem can again travel through course, feedback, and practice.
mapping: All three colored learning activities are completed as planned → None of the three sources is missing; the problem is not the absence of one form of learning
The queue shortens while the shelves simultaneously lose staffing → Real experience produces genuine feedback, but it does not automatically become complete judgment
The same decision card enters course review, Sister Zhou’s feedback, and the next shift → The three sources connect around one capability problem instead of being completed separately
“Make up 40 minutes” is crossed out while all three colors remain and arrows are added → The correction concerns mechanical allocation and fragmented use, not the rejection of any learning source
boundary: 70-20-10 does not prove that work experience is inherently more important than courses, nor does it prescribe a fixed development ratio for everyone. Some roles require more formal training; some capabilities depend more heavily on practice or high-quality feedback. Even when all three sources are present, simply “connecting” them will not automatically produce development if the wrong problem is chosen, feedback quality is poor, or work opportunities lack sufficient challenge.
reflection: For one capability you most want to develop now, do problems from experience actually enter feedback and formal learning, then return to the next round of practice?
